flags.html: This is a matching exercise, but the bank scores it as if A alone were the answer. The key line gives the full mapping; check yourself against every pair, not just the letter.

hippo-msk-Q65.html:
From 08 - Acute Monoarthritis and the MSK summary notes. An acute pseudogout (CPPD) attack is treated like an acute gout attack: NSAIDs (indomethacin), colchicine, or steroids (intra-articular or oral prednisone). What does not carry over from gout is urate lowering (allopurinol), which is for gout only.

  • A (colchicine) is on the notes' acute-attack list for pseudogout.
  • B, D are both listed: IA injection and a short oral prednisone taper.
  • C is an NSAID; a COXIB belongs to the same class as the indomethacin in the notes.

So on the notes, every option is an appropriate treatment for CPPD.

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: The key says colchicine is inappropriate because it is a gout drug. The MSK summary notes list colchicine for acute pseudogout attacks, and the Schulich MSK review notes it on the slide (SR slide 115), although the embedded pseudogout note leaves it out. Colchicine is used in CPPD, so no option here is clearly inappropriate. The key's distinction is allopurinol, not colchicine.

hippo-msk-Q69.html:
From 02 - Approach to Polyarthritis. The lecture's rule is flat: whenever the sacroiliac joint is involved, think seronegative spondyloarthropathy (ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic, IBD-associated, reactive). Axial disease with asymmetric large peripheral joints is their pattern, and inflammatory back pain (better with movement, worse in the second half of the night) goes with it.

  • A, B fail: CTD arthritis and RA are symmetric small- and large-joint peripheral diseases.
  • D fails: OA targets weight-bearing joints, the 1st CMC and DIPs; its spine disease is facet OA, not sacroiliitis.

hippo-neuro-Q16:
From 06 - Cranial Nerve Anatomy and Function. CN VIII carries two sensory functions, hearing and balance, and the note tests each: a hearing test, the Romberg sign, and assessment for nystagmus.

  • A, B are the hearing tests: 04 - Hearing Loss pairs Weber (lateralizes) with Rinne (separates conductive from sensorineural) and says to always do both.
  • C tests the vestibular half: an acute vestibular loss produces nystagmus.
  • D is listed for CN VIII too: with the eyes closed, balance rests on vestibular input plus proprioception, so a vestibular lesion can unmask a positive Romberg.
hippo-neuro-Q19:
From 07 - Facial Anatomy. The auriculotemporal nerve is a branch of V3 that runs with the superficial temporal artery and vein, supplying the skin in front of the ear, the temporal scalp and the TMJ.

  • A (frontal, V1) gives off the supraorbital nerve to the forehead.
  • B (infraorbital, V2) supplies the midface through the infraorbital foramen.
  • C (mental, V3) supplies the chin through the mental foramen.
  • D (great auricular, C2-C3) supplies the angle of the mandible and is the one facial territory outside the trigeminal nerve.
hippo-neuro-Q20:
From 07 - Facial Anatomy. The great auricular nerve comes from the cervical plexus (ventral rami of C2 and C3) and supplies the skin over the angle of the mandible, the one patch of the face the trigeminal nerve does not cover.

  • A (frontal, V1) is the forehead.
  • B (infraorbital, V2) is the midface and upper lip.
  • C (mental, V3) is the chin and lower lip, anterior to the angle.
  • E (auriculotemporal, V3) is in front of the ear and the temporal scalp.
hippo-neuro-Q21:
From 07 - Facial Anatomy. The sphincters are named for the opening they surround: orbicularis oris surrounds the lips and closes the mouth; it is orbicularis oculi that closes the eye. That makes C the incorrect pairing.

  • A is correct: frontalis (occipitofrontalis over the frontal bone) raises the eyebrows.
  • B is correct: zygomaticus major pulls the corners of the mouth up into a smile.
  • D is correct as the lecture states it: platysma helps depress the mandible.
  • E is correct: occipitalis moves the scalp.
hippo-neuro-Q22:
From 07 - Facial Anatomy. The muscles of mastication act on the TMJ and are supplied by V3, not the facial nerve. The lecture names masseter (strongly closes and protrudes the jaw) and temporalis (closes and retracts it).

  • B fails: the orbicularis muscles are facial-expression sphincters of the mouth and eye (CN VII).
  • C fails: the zygomatici raise the corners of the mouth.
  • D fails: buccinator helps chewing by keeping food between the teeth but is a muscle of facial expression; platysma is too.
hippo-neuro-Q23:
From 07 - Facial Anatomy. CN VII splits in the parotid into five branches, each matched to the muscle it supplies, and every pairing here matches the lecture:

  • A Temporal → occipitofrontalis (frontalis), plus the upper orbicularis oculi.
  • B Zygomatic → zygomaticus major, plus the lower orbicularis oculi.
  • C Buccal → buccinator, plus part of orbicularis oris.
  • D Marginal mandibular → the inferior orbicularis oris.
  • E Cervical → platysma.

D is the one to hesitate on: orbicularis oris has two supplies (buccal above, marginal mandibular below), so both pairings are correct.
hippo-neuro-Q45:
From 08 - Cortical Syndromes. Broca's area is in the inferior frontal lobe, next to motor cortex, so its aphasia is a motor (expressive) deficit. Wernicke's area is in the posterior temporal lobe, next to auditory cortex, so its aphasia is a sensory (receptive) deficit in understanding. Fluency does not follow comprehension: a Wernicke patient producing nonsense words is still fluent.

  • A swaps the deficits and puts Wernicke's in the parietal lobe.
  • B swaps both the lobes and the deficits.
  • D puts Broca's in the parietal lobe and gives Wernicke's the expressive deficit.
hippo-neuro-Q47:
From 11 - Neurophysiology of Vision. The lecture defines glaucoma as raised intraocular pressure compressing the axons of retinal ganglion cells, the axons that form the optic nerve. It takes peripheral vision first, giving "tunnel vision". (06 - Monocular Vision Impairment refines this: glaucoma is the optic neuropathy itself, and it can occur at normal pressure.)

  • A fails: cataract is clouding of the lens from misfolded proteins.
  • B fails: Horner syndrome is a sympathetic-chain lesion (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis), not a pressure problem.
  • C fails: macular degeneration is deposits or new vessels under the fovea, distorting central vision.
  • E fails: myopia is a refractive error.

hippo-neuro-Q48.html:
From 12 - Neuroanatomy of the Cortex. Memory is distributed:

  • A The hippocampus forms new memories and converts short-term to long-term; bilateral loss (patient H.M.) causes anterograde amnesia.
  • D The amygdala, anteromedial to it, has an integral role in emotion, learning and memory.
  • B, C The prefrontal cortex is a multimodal association area responsible for working memory, and association cortex links new input to memories of past experience.

All four count.

flags.title: B and C are only partly in the notes
flags.html: 12 - Neuroanatomy of the Cortex credits the prefrontal cortex with working memory but never names the medial frontal or ventromedial prefrontal cortex. Keying B and C as correct is reasonable, but it rests on treating them as prefrontal subregions, not on anything the note says about them specifically.

hippo-neuro-Q56:
From 11 - Neuroembryology. A newborn without a skull or the front of the brain is anencephaly: failed closure of the cranial neural tube, so parts of the brain and skull never form. There is no treatment, almost all affected babies die shortly after birth, and folic acid in pregnancy is preventive.

  • B fails: lissencephaly is a migration defect giving a smooth cortex with few gyri; the skull is there.
  • C fails: microlissencephaly is the same smooth brain with a small head at birth, still with a skull.
  • D fails: polymicrogyria is too many small folds, with the cortex reduced from 6 layers to 2-3.
hippo-neuro-Q65:
From 05 - Neuropathic Pain. The lecture opens by separating nociceptive pain (tissue injury, somatic or visceral) from neuropathic pain (a nervous-system lesion or dysfunction), and says the two are not treated the same way. NSAIDs target inflammatory tissue pain and are absent from its neuropathic list.

  • A is listed: amitriptyline, a TCA that also helps sleep and is the cheapest option.
  • C is listed: gabapentin, an anticonvulsant and the classic choice for postherpetic neuralgia.
  • D is listed: capsaicin, topical, applied 3x daily.
  • E is listed under "Other": cannabinoids.
hippo-neuro-Q90:
From 05 - Movement Disorders. The lecture's mnemonic for Parkinson's disease is TRAP: Tremor at rest, starting on one side; Rigidity, which increases with augmentation; Akinesia and bradykinesia (hard to start movement, slow movement); Postural instability (poor balance).

  • A fails: tumor, aphasia and paresthesia are not parkinsonian features.
  • B fails on P: paresis (weakness) is not a feature, since strength is preserved in PD.
  • D fails: tumor and "polyrheumatica" are distractors (polymyalgia rheumatica is a rheumatology diagnosis).
hippo-neuro-Q103:
From 06 - Monocular Vision Impairment. Glare and halos around lights that make night driving worse are the classic symptoms in the embedded cataract note. Cataract is opacity of the lens, the leading cause of reversible blindness, and fully treatable with lens replacement. At 55 it fits the age.

  • B fails: glaucoma is silent until late, then takes peripheral vision first. It does not cause glare.
  • C fails: vitreous hemorrhage (e.g., proliferative diabetic retinopathy) gives sudden floaters or vision loss, with dark mobile spots in the red reflex.
  • D fails because A fits.

The car accident is incidental; it is simply when the driving problem came up.
hippo-neuro-Q107:
From 04 - Hearing Loss. The lecture lists the drugs that damage cochlear hair cells or CN VIII: platinum chemotherapy (cisplatin, carboplatin), aminoglycosides, and loop diuretics (furosemide). Aspirin can cause a temporary, reversible ototoxicity.

  • A, B, C are all on that list individually, so the combined option that holds all three is right.
  • D fails: it leaves out the loop diuretics.

These drugs cause a sensorineural loss, so Weber lateralizes to the better ear.
hippo-neuro-Q108:
From 05 - Vertigo. In BPPV a loose otoconium drifts into a semicircular canal (usually the posterior canal, since it sits lowest). The note's features follow from that:

  • A is true: episodes are brief, under a minute, in the seconds-to-minutes row of the duration table.
  • B is true: attacks are triggered by head movement (looking up, rolling over in bed), and are diagnosed with Dix-Hallpike and cured with Epley.
  • C is false: BPPV is purely vestibular, with no hearing loss and no vision loss.

So D (A and B) is right, and E fails for including vision loss.

hippo-neuro-Q111.html:
From 06 - Approach to Headache. An aura is a transient, reversible neurologic disturbance that comes before or with the migraine. The migraine note gives the classic form as visual: photopsia and transient visual loss (B). A sensory aura, spreading numbness and tingling (C), is the other common type, though that goes beyond the note.

  • A fails: coma is an altered level of consciousness, a red flag for a secondary cause, not an aura.
  • D fails: fever with headache points to infection (e.g., meningitis), not migraine.

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: The key marks all four options, including coma and fever. Neither is a migraine aura: 06 - Approach to Headache and its migraine note describe the aura as visual (photopsia), and fever or reduced consciousness with headache are warning signs of something else. The defensible answer is B and C.

hippo-neuro-Q113:
From 01 - The Dying Patient and MAiD. Among the safeguards the lecture lists, two independent clinicians must certify eligibility (the note says two physicians), after a written request witnessed by an independent party.

  • A fails: patients must be at least 18 and mentally competent.
  • B fails: consent is given at the request and again at the time of MAiD, unless a waiver of final consent was signed (allowed only in the stream where natural death is reasonably foreseeable).
  • D fails: MAiD can happen at home, in long-term care or in hospital. Hospital is typical only when organ donation follows.

hippo-neuro-Q114.html:
From 08 - Pediatric Ophthalmology. A white reflex (leukocoria) means something white sits behind the pupil or in front of it, so anything opacifying the path of light can cause it. The lecture names retinoblastoma (the retinal cause that must not be missed) and congenital cataract (an anterior cause). Retinopathy of prematurity produces it when advanced disease leaves a scarred or detached retina.

  • A, B, C are each a cause, so D is right.

Any abnormal red reflex in a child needs urgent ophthalmology referral. Remember the one benign mimic: an off-axis light (~15°) can reflect off the optic nerve and look white.

flags.title: C is not in the notes
flags.html: 08 - Pediatric Ophthalmology names retinoblastoma and congenital cataract as causes of leukocoria but does not mention retinopathy of prematurity. That part is from general principles; verify it before relying on it.

hippo-neuro-Q11.html:
From 12 - Neuroanatomy of the Cortex. The sensory homunculus gives cortex to body parts by receptor density, not size, so the densely innervated face (lips, tongue) and hands (fingertips) get the largest areas of the postcentral gyrus. The motor homunculus follows the same logic for fine movement, and the hands dominate there too.

  • A fails: the hands are large but the arms are not.
  • B fails: legs and feet sit on a small strip on the medial surface (ACA territory).
  • D fails: the trunk is tiny; the genitals are represented but small.

hippo-neuro-Q12.html:
From 05 - Introduction to Neuroanatomy. The three planes: a coronal cut runs side to side, like a slice of bread, so both hemispheres, the ventricles and (further back) the hippocampi appear together, symmetric about the midline. An axial cut is parallel to the horizon. A sagittal cut runs front to back and shows one hemisphere in profile.

  • A would show a side-on profile with the corpus callosum as an arch.
  • C, D are the same plane (transverse is another name for axial), which is a hint that neither can be the single answer.

flags.title: The image is missing
flags.html: The source question showed a brain image that is not in the portal, so the key cannot be checked against it. The explanation gives the rules for telling the planes apart; the letter comes from the bank.

hippo-neuro-Q26.html:
From 01 - Neuroanatomy of the Brainstem, Basal Ganglia, and Diencephalon. Each disease targets a different part of the dopamine and basal ganglia circuit.

  • 1, Parkinson's → C, substantia nigra: the midbrain's dopamine-producing neurons are lost, the direct pathway becomes hypoactive, and thalamic output falls (bradykinesia).
  • 2, Huntington's → A, striatum: the caudate and putamen degenerate, the indirect pathway goes quiet, and thalamic output rises (a hyperkinetic disorder).
  • 3, Schizophrenia → B, nucleus accumbens: the accumbens is the ventral striatum, a limbic dopamine target. 07 - Introduction to Psychopharmacology ties positive symptoms to excess dopamine in the mesolimbic pathway.

The trap is that the accumbens is also striatum. Huntington's is a movement disorder of the dorsal striatum (caudate and putamen).

review.t: Neuroanatomy of the Brainstem, Basal Ganglia, and Diencephalon

hippo-neuro-Q29.html:
From 03 - Psychotic Disorders & Schizophrenia (Week 19). Positive symptoms are experiences people normally do not have, added on top of normal mental life. Negative symptoms are a loss of normal function.

  • A, B are positive symptoms. Hallucinations and delusions are the lecture's core examples, alongside disorganized thinking and excitement.
  • C, anhedonia (reduced pleasure) is a loss of function, so it is negative.
  • D, alogia (reduced spontaneous speech) is also negative.

The rest of the negative list is flattened affect, avolition, anergia, asociality, inattention and ambivalence. The split matters because first-generation antipsychotics treat only the positive symptoms.

hippo-neuro-Q37.html:
From 02 - Neuroanatomy of the Spinal Tracts and Cerebellum. Two of the three long tracts cross in the medulla. Only the pain pathway crosses as soon as it enters the cord.

  • Corticospinal → medulla: 90% of axons cross at the pyramidal decussation into the lateral corticospinal tract. The other 10% stay ipsilateral in the anterior tract.
  • Medial lemniscus → medulla: the second-order neurons in the nucleus gracilis and cuneatus send their axons across as the medial lemniscus.
  • Spinothalamic → spinal cord entry: the first-order neuron synapses in the dorsal horn at once, and the second-order axon crosses in the anterior white commissure.

This split is why a hemicord (Brown-Séquard) lesion causes ipsilateral loss of vibration and proprioception but contralateral loss of pain and temperature.

review.t: Neuroanatomy of the Spinal Tracts and Cerebellum

hippo-neuro-Q41.html:
From 10 - Approach to Localization. Once a lesion is placed in the brain, the lecture sorts it by signs that only one level can produce. Aphasia heads the list of cortical signs, followed by neglect, apraxia, cortical sensory loss (agraphesthesia, astereognosis) and isolated homonymous hemianopia. Language depends on the cortex of the dominant hemisphere.

  • B, subcortical lesions cause pure motor or pure sensory hemibody deficits (face = arm = leg) or ataxic hemiparesis, and language is spared.
  • C, brainstem lesions cause vertigo or diplopia plus another sign, or crossed face-versus-body sensory loss.

Do not confuse word-finding difficulty (aphasia) with slurred speech (dysarthria). Dysarthria can come from any of the three levels and leaves comprehension, naming, repetition and fluency intact.

hippo-neuro-Q43.html:
From 08 - Anatomy of the Cranial Cavity, and the cavernous sinus note. The contents of the cavernous sinus are the internal carotid artery (with its sympathetic plexus) and CN III, IV, V1, V2 and VI. That is why compression, whether by thrombus, pituitary mass or carotid aneurysm, causes ophthalmoplegia, orbital and facial pain, chemosis and trigeminal sensory loss.

  • B (CN IV), E (CN V2), F (ICA): all run through the sinus, so all are affected.
  • A, optic chiasm: not a content of the sinus.
  • C, CN VIII: runs in the internal acoustic meatus of the posterior fossa.
  • D, CN V3: leaves through the foramen ovale and does not pass through the sinus.

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: The key includes A, optic chiasm. Neither 08 - Anatomy of the Cranial Cavity nor the cavernous sinus note places the optic pathway in the sinus. Its contents are the ICA and CN III, IV, V1, V2 and VI, so the supported answer is B, E, F. The cavernous sinus note mislabels the ophthalmic nerve as “CN II”, which may be how the chiasm got into the key.

hippo-neuro-Q46.html:
From 11 - Neurophysiology of Vision. Accommodation is the lens changing shape to keep the image focused on the retina. The ciliary muscles change its shape through the suspensory fibres. When they contract, the lens rounds up for near vision. When they relax, the lens flattens for distance.

  • B: the iris and pupil control how much light enters (the pupillary light reflex), not focus.
  • C: only half right. The pupil constricts along with accommodation (both are driven by CN III through the ciliary ganglion) but does no focusing itself.
  • D: light passes through the cornea first, but the lecture gives the focusing change to the lens.
  • E: the fovea receives the image, and the posterior chamber is a fluid space.

hippo-neuro-Q54.html:
From 02 - Neuroanatomy of the Spinal Tracts and Cerebellum. Pain, temperature and crude touch travel in the spinothalamic tract. Its first-order neuron synapses in the dorsal horn right away. The second-order axon crosses in the anterior white commissure at the level of entry, then ascends on the opposite side to the thalamus.

  • B: wrong tract. The dorsal columns carry fine touch, vibration and proprioception.
  • C: right tract, wrong crossing point. The medulla is where the dorsal column pathway crosses, as the medial lemniscus.
  • D: accurate for the dorsal columns, but they do not carry pain or temperature.

Learn each tract together with where it crosses, because the crossing point is what localizes a cord lesion.

review.t: Neuroanatomy of the Spinal Tracts and Cerebellum

hippo-neuro-Q61.html:
From Schulich Reviews - Neuro (01 - Approach to Head Injuries). Severe head trauma starts with the ABCDE primary survey under C-spine precautions, with intubation if GCS is below 8, followed by a STAT CT. CT is fast enough to find a hematoma that needs surgery. MRI takes too long and is impractical in an unstable trauma patient, so it comes later, once the patient is stable and the CT is done.

  • A: protecting the airway and spine is the first step.
  • B, C: large-bore IV access and bloodwork are part of circulation in any major trauma resuscitation. The review names the survey, not these specifics.
  • D: STAT non-contrast CT head is the first-line imaging.

hippo-neuro-Q62.html:
From Schulich Reviews - Neuro (01 - Approach to Head Injuries and 10 - Neurosurgical Emergencies). A is false because it gives the mixed-density appearance to the wrong lesion. Contusions show mixed high and low density on CT. A traumatic intracerebral hemorrhage is a well-defined, homogeneous hyperdense bleed. The first half of A is correct: subdurals are crescent-shaped and concave.

  • B, true: raccoon eyes, Battle's sign and CSF rhinorrhea or otorrhea are signs of a basilar skull fracture.
  • C, true: subdurals come from acceleration/deceleration injury tearing the bridging veins.
  • D, true: the lecture groups traumatic SAH with diffuse axonal injury and concussion as diffuse injuries.
  • E, true: coup injury is under the impact and contrecoup is opposite it.

hippo-neuro-Q64.html:
From 02 - Multiple Sclerosis (the embedded MS note). Diagnosis requires dissemination in time and space and the exclusion of mimics. MRI shows focal areas of inflammation, and lumbar puncture finds oligoclonal bands in about 95% (sensitive, not specific). C is therefore true.

  • A: right sex (3:1 female) and right ancestry, but the wrong age. MS most often affects people aged 20 to 40.
  • B: the key corrects this to older men. The lecture does not tie primary progressive MS to young men or to genetics, and twin concordance is only 20-30%.
  • D: vitamin D deficiency (or low sun exposure) is a listed environmental risk, along with EBV, smoking, adolescent obesity and shift work.
  • E: disease-modifying and symptomatic therapy are correct, but there is no myelin grafting. The only experimental therapies named are fecal and bone-marrow transplant.

hippo-psych-Q1:
From 04 - Esophageal Dysphagia (PoM 1, Gastroenterology Week 10). This question is GI, not psychiatry. The first history question is whether solids alone get stuck, or both solids and liquids. A fixed narrowing blocks only solids, while a motility failure affects both.

  • A, mechanical: i, iv. A Schatzki ring is a distal mucosal ring that causes intermittent solid-food dysphagia. Eosinophilic esophagitis (rings, vertical furrows, food bolus impaction in young atopic males) is grouped with the structural causes.
  • B, motility: ii, iii, v, vi. Jackhammer esophagus (high-amplitude repetitive contractions), scleroderma (scarred, thickened wall), diffuse esophageal spasm (simultaneous non-propulsive contractions, the corkscrew) and achalasia (the LES fails to relax, the bird's beak).

Motility disorders are diagnosed by manometry, not endoscopy.
hippo-psych-Q10:
From 11 - Depression and Anxiety in Medical Illnesses. Major depression is common across chronic medical illness, and the lecture stresses that the link runs both ways. Illness raises the risk of depression, and MDD is itself a risk factor for diabetes, coronary disease, stroke, cancer and dementia. The prevalence figures it gives include stroke 22-50%, cancer 18-39%, Parkinson's 10-37%, diabetes 9-27%, MI 15-19% and rheumatoid arthritis about 13%.

  • A-D are each correct alone, so choosing only one misses the point. E is the only complete answer.

Epilepsy, lupus and liver disease are not on the lecture's list, but they follow the same pattern of chronic neurological, inflammatory and systemic illness. Screen chronically ill patients for depression. In diabetes, for example, having both conditions causes more disability than either one alone.
hippo-psych-Q13:
From 01 - Diagnosis in Psychiatry. The DSM-5 dropped the multi-axial structure, but the lecture keeps it as a reference. The axes run from the disorder outward to the patient's context:

  • Axis I: clinical disorders, including major mental disorders and learning disorders. A is correct.
  • Axis II: personality disorders and intellectual disability, the lifelong conditions that underlie Axis I. B describes Axis IV.
  • Axis III: acute medical conditions and physical disorders. C describes Axis II.
  • Axis IV: psychosocial and environmental factors. D describes Axis V.
  • Axis V: assessment of functioning. E describes Axis III.

Every distractor describes a real axis under the wrong number, so the question tests the numbering itself.
hippo-psych-Q8:
From 10 - Psychotherapies in Mood and Anxiety Disorders. Each description names a feature that only one therapy has:

  • A, psychodynamic → iv: unstructured free association, a neutral “blank screen” therapist, interpretation of transference, and defences worked through by clarifying and confronting.
  • B, DBT → v: developed specifically for borderline personality disorder. It uses behavioural chain analysis and is delivered as individual therapy, group skills training, phone coaching and therapist consultation.
  • C, CBT → ii: schemas, automatic thoughts and cognitive distortions, tracked with thought records.
  • D, behavioural activation → i: act before you feel better, using activity scheduling rated for accomplishment and pleasure.
  • E, IPT → iii: short, present-focused work on role disputes, role transitions, grief and interpersonal deficits. Transference is deliberately not addressed, which is the clearest contrast with iv.

hippo-psych-Q23.html:
From 07 - Approach to ADHD (the DSM-5 criteria in the embedded ADHD note). The DSM-5 splits ADHD symptoms into two lists. Careless mistakes belong to the inattention list (not attending to details, making careless errors in schoolwork or at work), not to hyperactivity-impulsivity.

  • A: blurting out an answer before the question is finished is an impulsivity item.
  • B: leaving the seat when staying seated is expected is a hyperactivity item.
  • C: fidgeting, tapping or squirming is a hyperactivity item.
  • E: being unable to play quietly is a hyperactivity item.

A diagnosis needs 6 symptoms from a list (5 from age 17) lasting 6 months, with onset before age 12 and symptoms in 2 or more settings. Inattentive presentations are harder to spot and more common in girls.

hippo-psych-Q28:
From 08 - Speech and Language Disorders (the embedded developmental language disorder note). Language disorder is highly heritable, with an incidence of 20-40% in families with a history of it.

  • A: reversed. It is more common in boys (2-3:1).
  • B: bilingual children with a language disorder show a similar pattern in both languages. The disorder affects language ability in general, not one particular language.
  • C: only about 40-50% of late talkers catch up on their own, so waiting is not a safe default.

Before making the diagnosis, rule out hearing loss with formal audiology and arrange an SLP assessment.

hippo-psych-Q30.html:
From 09 - Autism Spectrum Disorder & Intellectual Disabilities (Management of Developmental Disabilities). No drug treats ASD itself. Medication targets behaviours that interfere with daily life. Aggression is usually triggered by frustration and reflects poor emotional regulation and impulse control. For it, the lecture lists antipsychotics first, then anticonvulsants, then stimulants or atomoxetine. Risperidone is the only antipsychotic among the options.

  • A, fluoxetine: an SSRI, and not one of the lecture's options for aggression.
  • B, benzodiazepine: not on the list.
  • D, amitriptyline: a tricyclic, also not on the list.

Medication supplements non-drug supports rather than replacing them. For ASD the most important of these is early intensive behavioural intervention.

hippo-psych-Q31:
From 10 - Disruptive Behavior Disorders. The lecture lists chronic physical illness or disability among the individual and psychological risk factors for ODD and conduct disorder. Each of the other three options reverses a listed risk factor:

  • B: male sex is the risk factor (possibly through testosterone).
  • C: low birth weight is the risk, along with antenatal and perinatal complications.
  • D: the risk is underactivity of inhibitory regions (frontal lobe, amygdala, hippocampus). Together with autonomic hyporeactivity, it means less anxiety about consequences.

The remaining risks are family factors (parental antisocial behaviour, harsh or inconsistent discipline, maltreatment) and social factors (low SES, delinquent peers, bullying).
hippo-psych-Q33:
From 05 - Personality Disorders. The three clusters:

  • Cluster A (“mad”), odd and eccentric: paranoid, schizoid, schizotypal.
  • Cluster B (“bad”), dramatic and erratic: antisocial, borderline, histrionic, narcissistic.
  • Cluster C (“sad”), anxious and fearful: avoidant, dependent, obsessive-compulsive.

A, C and D (borderline, histrionic, antisocial) are all Cluster B. Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder is Cluster C, so it is the one that does not belong. Cluster C disorders share emotional inhibition, avoidance of interpersonal contact, self-blame and guilt, which is the opposite of the outward-directed, dramatic Cluster B.
hippo-psych-Q34:
From 05 - Personality Disorders. Personality disorders affect about 11% of the general population. The lecture names borderline personality disorder as the most common (28%), with dependent personality disorder next (15%).

  • A, B: antisocial and narcissistic are Cluster B like borderline, but the lecture gives neither as the most common.
  • D, E: schizotypal and paranoid are Cluster A. Cluster A is the least studied, partly because these patients rarely seek treatment.

Because BPD is so common, its treatment also has the most evidence. DBT is first line, following “skills not pills”, with medication used only for comorbidities.

hippo-psych-Q35.html:
From 04 - Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (the embedded PTSD note). Criterion A is the gatekeeper: exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury or sexual violence. The exposure can be direct, witnessed in person, learned of happening to someone close (if violent or accidental), or repeated exposure to aversive details at work. Nearly dying in a house fire is direct exposure to threatened death.

  • A, C, D: failing an exam, fighting with a friend and being suspended are distressing, but none threatens life or physical safety. They cannot meet Criterion A however severe the reaction.

If the stressor falls short of Criterion A but symptoms follow it, consider adjustment disorder instead.

hippo-psych-Q36.html:
From 03 - Management of Anxiety Disorders and OCD, and the 1st-line list in the PTSD note. Four drugs carry a PTSD tick in the lecture's table: fluoxetine, paroxetine, sertraline and venlafaxine. The PTSD note lists the same four as 1st line, and they are exactly option A.

  • D is the trap. Three of its four drugs are right, but citalopram is ticked for panic disorder and OCD, not PTSD.
  • B: a tricyclic, an antipsychotic, bupropion and topiramate. None of them is first line.
  • C: olanzapine and mirtazapine are not first line, and fluvoxamine (listed twice) is ticked for social anxiety, panic and OCD, not PTSD.

Trauma-focused psychotherapy (cognitive processing therapy, EMDR) is also first line.

review.t: Management of Anxiety Disorders and OCD

hippo-psych-Q39:
From 06 - Dissociation and Dissociative Disorders, with the DES-II note. The Dissociative Experiences Scale II is a 28-item self-report questionnaire designed to measure dissociation. The answers are averaged, and a score of 30 or more means high dissociation. It is the scale listed for investigating depersonalization-derealization disorder.

  • A, PHQ-9: measures depression severity.
  • B, Y-BOCS: measures obsessive-compulsive symptom severity.
  • C, MMSE: a cognitive screen, used for dementia or delirium.

Each distractor is a well-known instrument for a different disorder, so the question comes down to matching the scale to what it measures.
hippo-psych-Q41:
From 01 - Anxiety Disorders. The lecture's risk factors are family history, a personal history of anxiety or mood disorders (depression, bipolar disorder, ADHD), childhood stress or trauma, chronic medical illness (asthma, diabetes, obesity, cardiovascular disease), behavioural inhibition, and being female.

  • A, B, C, D: each is on that list, so each is a risk factor.
  • E: being male reverses the listed sex risk, so it is the one that is not a risk factor.

Compare disruptive behaviour disorders, where male sex is the risk. Sex risks that flip between lectures are a common exam trap.
hippo-psych-Q45:
From 03 - Management of Anxiety Disorders and OCD (the “SSRIS” side-effect list) and In-Class - Mood Disorders. The common SSRI side effects are sexual dysfunction, sleep disturbance, restlessness, indigestion and serotonin syndrome. The in-class session names trazodone as the adjunct for insomnia, so C is the pairing the course teaches.

  • A: SSRI sexual dysfunction is serotonergic and affects libido. The fix is switching to bupropion, which has no serotonin effect, not adding a benzodiazepine (or sildenafil).
  • B: bupropion is matched to the wrong side effect. It treats sexual dysfunction, not restlessness.
  • D: the lecture gives no treatment for SSRI indigestion, so this is not a pairing it teaches.
hippo-psych-Q46:
From 03 - Management of Anxiety Disorders and OCD. The four types of exposure differ in what triggers the fear. Virtual exposure uses a computer simulation for situations that are hard to face in real life. The lecture's examples are thunderstorms and flying, and a simulated war for combat PTSD applies the same idea.

  • A: hyperventilating to bring on trembling is interoceptive because it provokes a body sensation. It is not situational.
  • B: returning to the place of the mugging is situational (in vivo), and it is the lecture's own PTSD example. It is not interoceptive.
  • C: running on the spot to produce panic symptoms is also interoceptive. Imaginal exposure happens in the mind only and is used most for PTSD.

A, B and C each describe a real exposure under the wrong label.
hippo-psych-Q49:
From 02 - The Child Welfare System. Under the Ontario Child and Family Services Act, health professionals must report all suspected abuse or neglect, and this duty overrides other statutes that would prevent disclosure. A report gives immunity from civil action unless it is made maliciously or without reasonable cause. Unexplained bruising together with a hostile, evasive parent is reasonable cause.

  • A: backwards. The legal risk comes from not reporting: criminal prosecution, civil liability, CPSO discipline, and fines of up to $5000 in Ontario.
  • B: the parent's consent is not needed, because the duty overrides confidentiality.
  • D: the right action for the wrong reason. The threshold is suspicion, not certainty, and investigating is CAS's job.
hippo-psych-Q50:
From 02 - The Child Welfare System. Subsection 57(5) of the Child and Family Services Act sets the order of priority for placing an Indigenous child before they are made a Society or Crown ward, unless there is a substantial reason to place them elsewhere:

  • 1st, C: a member of the child's extended family.
  • 2nd, B: a member of the child's band or Indigenous community.
  • 3rd, A: another Indigenous family.

The order moves outward from the child's own family, to their community, to Indigenous families more broadly. It follows the 1985 amendments that recognized Indigenous peoples' right to provide their own child and family services in a way that respects their culture and their concept of extended family. The band also receives the child's assessment reports and must be notified of any plan for adoption.
hippo-psych-Q53:
From 04 - Treatment of Psychotic Disorders and 07 - Introduction to Psychopharmacology. Each pathway has its own dopamine problem. Excess dopamine in the mesolimbic pathway puts the limbic system on overdrive, which disrupts salience and produces hallucinations and delusions. This is why antipsychotics block D2 there. Disruption of the mesocortical pathway, classically a dopamine deficit, impairs the system for learning, motivation and organizing behaviour, which shows up as negative and cognitive symptoms.

  • A, B: the correct pairings.
  • C: puts a deficit in the mesolimbic pathway, where the problem is excess.
  • D: puts an excess in the mesocortical pathway, where there is too little.

This is why first-generation antipsychotics, which block D2 throughout the brain, treat only the positive symptoms.
hippo-psych-Q54:
From 04 - Treatment of Psychotic Disorders. First-generation drugs are high-potency D2 blockers. Second-generation drugs cause fewer muscle side effects but more metabolic ones.

  • A, true: clozapine is the most effective antipsychotic, especially for treatment-resistant psychosis. It carries serious risks including agranulocytosis, so it requires monitoring. Haloperidol is first generation.
  • B, true: the lecture lists extrapyramidal effects and hypotension for first-generation drugs like haloperidol. Second-generation drugs like olanzapine were designed to cause fewer muscle side effects.
  • C, true: quetiapine is second generation, and the lecture highlights that class's metabolic and cardiovascular harms (weight gain, metabolic syndrome, bloodwork every 6 months).
  • D, false: reversed. Clozapine is one of the least dopamine-blocking antipsychotics, and haloperidol is the high-potency one.

Second-generation drugs are no more effective overall. Clozapine is the exception.
hippo-psych-Q61:
From 01 - Sleep Disorders. Match each EEG signature to its stage:

  • D, REM → 1: low-voltage fast activity with sawtooth waves, plus vivid dreaming, muscle atonia and rapid eye movements. It is thought to help memory consolidation.
  • A, N1 → 2: the transition from wakefulness, as alpha waves give way to low-voltage mixed-frequency (theta) waves. Only 2-5% of sleep, and easily interrupted.
  • B, N2 → 3: sleep spindles and K-complexes, linked to memory consolidation. At 45-55% of sleep, it is the largest share.
  • C, N3 → 4: high-voltage slow (delta) waves, daily brain recovery and growth hormone secretion. It is the hardest stage to wake from and is concentrated in the first third of the night.

Anchor each stage on one unique feature: alpha to theta (N1), spindles (N2), delta (N3), sawtooth (REM).

hippo-psych-Q62.html:
The notes do not cover this. 01 - Sleep Disorders gives the normal EEG of each stage, which is enough to rule out B-D. The finding classically described in fibromyalgia and chronic pain is alpha-wave intrusion into NREM sleep (“alpha-delta sleep”). The waking alpha rhythm keeps breaking into sleep, so sleep is light and unrefreshing.

  • B: spindles and K-complexes define N2, not N3.
  • C: large delta waves define N3. REM shows low-voltage fast activity.
  • D: sawtooth waves belong to REM. N1 is alpha giving way to theta.

Each distractor puts a real waveform in the wrong stage.

flags.title: Not covered by the notes
flags.html: No lecture note covers alpha intrusion; the reasoning is from general principles. Verify it before relying on it. Classic descriptions put the intrusion in slow-wave (N3) sleep rather than N2, so the option's stage label is loose, but A is still the only option that is not a stage mismatch.

hippo-psych-Q67.html:
From 01 - Sleep Disorders. The lecture gives three tiers of OSA treatment. The gold standard is positive airway pressure, either bi-level or continuous, which holds the airway open. A dental appliance (mandibular advancement) can help. Uvulopalatopharyngoplasty is the third-line surgical option.

  • A: CPAP, the gold standard.
  • B: a mandibular advancement device is the dental appliance.
  • C: UPPP, third line.
  • D: the lecture names BiPAP alongside CPAP as the gold standard, so it does not rule BiPAP out.

On this lecture, all four are defensible treatment options.

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: The bank marks only A correct, but its key line reads “A. B.C; BiPAP is not indicated in OSA”, which implies A, B and C. 01 - Sleep Disorders supports B and C. It also contradicts the comment on BiPAP, because it names bi-level or continuous positive airway pressure as the gold standard. On the lecture, A, B, C and D are all treatment options.

hippo-psych-Q84:
From 06 - Sexual Disorders and Paraphilias. People distressed by paraphilic interests are often referred to general mental health services first, but those referrals end up with forensic psychiatrists. The lecture calls sexual behaviour, deviance, offending and paraphilias a “super subspecialty” practised by some forensic psychiatrists. Forensic psychiatry is psychiatry plus law: assessing risk, managing sex offenders and giving expert testimony in court.

  • B, general psychiatry: where the referral often starts, not where the patient is treated.
  • A, child and C, liaison psychiatry: the lecture gives neither a role here.

The lecture also draws a distinction worth keeping: most people with paraphilias never offend, and not all sex offenders have a paraphilia. Psychological therapy is the gold-standard treatment.
hippo-psych-Q86:
From 07 - Management of Cognitive Disorders and Dementia. Dementia can produce almost any psychiatric symptom. The lecture groups the behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia (BPSD) into three types:

  • Affective: depression, anxiety, elation or disinhibition, apathy.
  • Behavioural: irritability, agitation or aggression, wandering, sleep disturbance, sexual disinhibition, vocalizations.
  • Psychotic: hallucinations of any kind, and delusions. Delusions are most often persecutory, which is what suspiciousness reflects.

A to D each fit a category, so the answer is E. The pattern shifts with the type of dementia: behavioural symptoms in frontotemporal, visual hallucinations in Lewy body, depression or apathy in vascular, and persecutory delusions in Alzheimer's.

hippo-psych-Q12.html:
From 06 - Pharmacology of Antidepressants and 07 - Introduction to Psychopharmacology. Sort each drug by which transmitter it leaves in the synapse:

  • SSRIs (A) block serotonin reuptake only: SERT (i).
  • SNRIs (E) inhibit both serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake: SERT + NET (i, ii).
  • TCAs (C) such as amitriptyline and clomipramine are also serotonin + norepinephrine reuptake blockers (i, ii). Their muscarinic, histamine and α1 blockade explains the side effects, not the antidepressant effect.
  • Bupropion (F), the NDRI, inhibits dopamine and norepinephrine reuptake: NET + DAT (ii, iii). That is why it spares weight and sexual function.
  • Amphetamine (B) is the dopaminergic stimulant: DAT (iii).
  • Tiagabine (D) is the odd one out, an anticonvulsant that blocks GABA reuptake: GAT1 (iv).

flags.title: Not covered by the notes
flags.html: The notes give the SSRI, SNRI and NDRI mechanisms but never name the transporters. The TCA transporter profile, amphetamine's action at DAT and tiagabine's block of GAT1 are not in them; those three come from general pharmacology. Verify them before relying on it.

hippo-psych-Q3.html:
From 07 - Introduction to Psychopharmacology. D is false because it describes an ionotropic receptor. Metabotropic receptors are G-protein-coupled and act through second messengers, so their effect is slower and longer-lasting. Only ligand-gated ion channels change membrane polarization directly for a fast onset; for serotonin, that is the single ionotropic subtype, 5-HT3.

  • A is true: NMDA receptors are glutamate-gated channels (Ca2+ influx), and glutamate is the main excitatory transmitter (08 - Pharmacotherapy of Cognitive Enhancers).
  • B is true: both monoamines are broken down by MAO and packaged into vesicles by VMAT, so drugs at either site affect both.
  • C is true: benzodiazepines open GABA-A chloride channels and reduce neuronal firing. That is the basis of their sedative, anticonvulsant and anesthetic uses.

flags.title: Not covered by the notes
flags.html: The notes name metabotropic (G-protein-coupled) and ionotropic (ligand-gated) receptors only in FoM physiology, without their speed of onset. 5-HT3 and VMAT do not appear in the notes. That part of the reasoning is from general principles, so verify it before relying on it.

hippo-psych-Q7.html:
From 09 - Bipolar Disorders and its Schulich review. Three features make a depressive episode more likely to be bipolar. The first is early onset: bipolar I averages 25 years, and most patients start earlier, with an early-onset group around 17. The second is atypical features, meaning hyperphagia with weight gain and hypersomnia. The third is psychotic features, and multiple recurrent episodes point the same way.

  • B: long episodes of over 6 months fit unipolar depression. Bipolar depressive episodes tend to be shorter and more frequent.
  • D: initial insomnia with poor appetite is the typical unipolar pattern. Bipolar depression leans toward hypersomnia instead.

flags.title: Not covered by the notes
flags.html: The review lists early onset, multiple episodes and hyperphagia/hypersomnia as bipolar features. The notes do not cover psychotic features, episode duration or initial insomnia as discriminators; those come from general principles (the usual bipolarity indicators). Verify them before relying on it.

hippo-psych-Q26.html:
From 08 - Speech and Language Disorders. A lisp is an articulation disorder, meaning difficulty producing particular speech sounds. It is a speech finding in its own right and not a cause of learning disability, so it is the odd one out.

  • Genetics (A): learning and neurodevelopmental disorders cluster in families.
  • Prenatal alcohol (B): alcohol is a teratogen, and the intellectual disability note lists it among prenatal causes of impaired development.
  • Low birthweight (D): prematurity and low birthweight raise the risk of neurodevelopmental and learning problems.

flags.title: Not covered by the notes
flags.html: No lecture note lists risk factors for learning disability. The lecture supports the lisp as an articulation disorder, and the intellectual disability note supports alcohol as a teratogen. Genetics and low birthweight as risk factors are from general principles, so verify them before relying on it.

hippo-psych-Q29.html:
From 09 - Autism Spectrum Disorder & Intellectual Disabilities. ASD and intellectual disability share a work-up. The lecture's investigations put genetic testing with a chromosomal microarray first (a karyotype is not helpful), plus fragile X testing, since fragile X is the most common genetic cause. ASD is also more common in genetic syndromes such as fragile X and tuberous sclerosis, so a diagnosis of ASD warrants genetic testing.

  • A: ASD is neurodevelopmental and present from the early developmental period. It is not degenerative; regression points to Rett syndrome.
  • C: this is backwards. An increased head circumference (>97th percentile) is the listed risk factor.
  • D: about 33% have intellectual disability, not 75%.

hippo-psych-Q32.html:
From 10 - Disruptive Behavior Disorders. Conduct disorder is a repetitive pattern of violating other people's rights: theft, lying, violence, destruction of property and serious rule-breaking. Its limited prosocial emotions specifier describes the callous-unemotional picture: lack of remorse or guilt, a callous lack of empathy, and shallow or deficient affect. Guilt and remorse are the opposite of that picture.

  • A: a callous lack of empathy is a specifier feature.
  • C: flat affect corresponds to shallow or deficient affect.
  • D: theft belongs to the deceitfulness-or-theft criterion cluster.

hippo-psych-Q37.html:
From 04 - Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder. PTSD requires the intrusion, avoidance, negative cognition/mood and arousal clusters to last more than 1 month. The same picture lasting 3 days to 1 month is acute stress disorder. The lecture's 3-month figures are different facts: symptoms usually begin within 3 months of the trauma, and about half of patients recover within 3 months.

  • 1 week (A) falls in the acute stress disorder window.
  • 6 months (B) is the delayed expression specifier, used when full criteria are not met until 6 months after the event. It is not the duration criterion.
  • 12 weeks (C) and 3 months (D) are the same interval, and neither is the duration criterion.

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: The key gives D (3 months). Both 04 - Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder and the Schulich review put the duration criterion at more than 1 month, and no option offers that. The 3-month figure is when symptoms usually begin, and it was the old DSM-IV cut-off between acute and chronic PTSD, which is probably where the key comes from. C and D also name the same interval. Treat the question as flawed: for an exam, the answer is more than 1 month.

hippo-psych-Q38.html:
From 06 - Dissociation and Dissociative Disorders. The lecture names three DSM disorders outside the dissociative disorders that include dissociation as a symptom:

  • Borderline personality disorder (A): transient, stress-related, severe dissociative symptoms are a criterion.
  • PTSD (B): the dissociative subtype.
  • Panic disorder (C): derealization and depersonalization are possible panic attack symptoms.

Narcissistic personality disorder (D) has no dissociative criterion. ASD (E) is defined by social-communication deficits and restricted, repetitive behaviour. The lecture mentions schizophrenia, eating disorders, mood disorders and OCD only as research associations.

hippo-psych-Q40.html: From 06 - Dissociation and Dissociative Disorders and the DES-II note. The Dissociative Experiences Scale is a 28-item self-report questionnaire, scored as the average of all items. A score of 30 or more marks high dissociation. That makes 30 (B) the cut-off, and 40 (D) or anything near them the clinical range: none of these is a population average. The general non-clinical population averages about 11, far below the cut-off.

flags.title: Not covered by the notes
flags.html: The notes give the DES-II's scoring and its cut-off of 30 or more for high dissociation, but not the non-clinical average of about 11. That figure is from general sources, so verify it before relying on it.

hippo-psych-Q42.html:
From 01 - Anxiety Disorders (panic disorder). Panic disorder cannot be diagnosed when the attacks are attributable to a substance or another medical condition. The lecture lists these mimics by system, and every option is on the list:

  • Endocrine: hypo- and hyperthyroidism (A), plus hypoglycemia and pheochromocytoma.
  • Substances: caffeine (B), alcohol, nicotine, stimulants.
  • Hematological: anemia (C) and vitamin B12 deficiency (D).
  • Cardio/respiratory: COPD (E), asthma, arrhythmias, heart failure, coronary artery disease.

That is why the suggested bloodwork includes TSH and a serum B12 before anxiety is labelled primary.

hippo-psych-Q43.html:
From 02 - Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder. The median age of onset of OCD is 19 years. About 21% begin in childhood, before age 10, and that early-onset group is more likely to be male and to have a tic disorder. That is why onset is earlier in men overall.

  • 7 (A) belongs to the childhood-onset minority, not the median.
  • 15 (B) and 25 (C) sound plausible but are not the lecture's figure.

hippo-psych-Q47.html:
From 01 - Eating Disorders. Refeeding syndrome is a potentially fatal complication of refeeding severely malnourished patients, and the lecture names hypophosphatemia as its hallmark. Starvation depletes total-body phosphate while the serum level stays normal. Once carbohydrate returns, insulin drives phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells, and the deficit shows (refeeding syndrome note).

  • Hypomagnesemia (B) occurs too, but it is not the defining abnormality.
  • Hyperkalemia (C) is backwards: potassium moves into cells, so hypokalemia results.
  • Diuresis (D): the fluid risk is overload, which is why fluids are given carefully.

hippo-psych-Q51.html:
From 03 - Psychotic Disorders & Schizophrenia (schizoaffective disorder). Both diagnoses combine psychosis with mood episodes, so timing is what separates them. Schizoaffective disorder requires delusions or hallucinations for at least 2 weeks in the absence of a major mood episode, with mood episodes present for most of the illness. A mood disorder with psychotic features has psychosis only during the mood episodes.

  • B reverses the rule.
  • C: psychosis during mania occurs in both conditions, so on its own it points to bipolar with psychotic features, not schizoaffective disorder.
  • D: psychosis during an episode does not discriminate either. Only psychosis outside the episodes settles the question.

hippo-psych-Q76.html:
From 09 - Autism Spectrum Disorder & Intellectual Disabilities and the syndrome notes. Each genetic cause of intellectual disability has a recognisable behavioural phenotype:

  • Angelman (A) → jerky movement (II): ataxic movement with a characteristically happy demeanour.
  • Williams (B) → hyperverbalisation (I): an overfriendly, talkative child whose verbal fluency outruns their cognition.
  • Prader-Willi (C) → neonatal hypotonia (III): a floppy newborn.
  • Fragile X (D) → anxiety and agitation (IV): social anxiety is prominent. Fragile X is the most common genetic cause of intellectual disability.

flags.title: Not covered by the notes
flags.html: The lecture lists fragile X as a cause of intellectual disability but not the behavioural phenotypes. The Angelman, Prader-Willi and fragile X notes support three pairings. The notes have no Williams syndrome note, so that pairing is from general principles; verify it before relying on it.
